full_text:
Interviewer:	When did you start your placement?

Subject:	Er, 21st of June.

Interviewer:	You’ve been here ages now then, haven’t you?

Subject:	Nearly done.

Interviewer:	Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

Subject:	They make water meters basically, um, for all different kinds of applications, some domestic, the kind of thing that you find outside your house, and some more industrial things that are for big power plants and that sort of thing, but only water at this company.

Interviewer:	Okay. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Um, it’s been really good. I think, um, you get some old timers that do treat you a bit differently, but I think that’s just because they’re older. Um, it’s quite amusing, I mean you’ve seen the number of doors there are here; everyone opens doors for me (inaudible) but I've certainly been treated with respect and what have you.

Interviewer:	Okay, we’ll come back to that sort of stuff later. Most of the questions I’ve got are about how the placement’s going and how you think it relates to your course and stuff like that. So how useful do you think that your course has been to the work that you’re doing so far?

Subject:	Not at all really it has to be said. Um, mainly the one thing that I’ve found useful from the course has been, um, the modelling that I’ve been doing, um, using computer packaging, but even that was so basic that I – as soon as I came here I was told, ‘Well, you know what, you can do it that way, but it’s not the best way to do it’ and you know, when you get into industry things are a bit more complicated and you have to really think more about what you’re doing and you don’t get these simple problems that you get at university; everything’s a lot more difficult and detailed and – because at the end of the day you’re going to be making tooling from this that’s got to make that product, so it has to be spot on and things from down to drawing etiquette and technique, we’re following British standards and to, um, just the technical ability to be able to model the sophistication of the parts, it’s just a bit extreme. But other than that I’ve not – not really use anything from my course. I’ve been mainly doing things, um, to do with the business management and project management and sort of brand awareness, so that’s more marketing and looking at that. So I’ve been doing – chopping and changing between all sorts of different things. (inaudible)

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s anything like the more generic skills from uni that you’ve used, like communication and organisation skills?

Subject:	I would say that they pale in comparison to the type of communication and, um, patience you need in a working environment. I’ve never met such a diverse amount of people and had to treat each one of them completely differently, because some people take things a little bit more seriously than others and some people, um, you have to be quite careful because if you don’t, I mean some people in here there’s a big joke, don’t go to this certain person because they will talk to you for hours and hours and hours and you’ve just got to be very tactful about the way you kind of say, ‘Well that’s nice, thank you for your information, but I really need to get on and do my work right now’. Things like that and doing presentations to the directors of the company and the directors of marketing and all this kind of stuff, it’s just nerve wracking and you don’t realise how much pressure gets put on you when you’re put in that sort of situation and you don’t know how you’ll cope until you actually do it. So it’s all about preparation.

Interviewer:	So is there anything that you wish you had learnt at uni before you came on placement?

Subject:	Um, I wish that, um, there were several things that I found out here which would have made my life so much easier at university. Things – things, a lot about, um, mainly the software that – simple, little things, I can’t even – there are so many of them, even just using Word. I mean how much do you write on Word and there are all these different functions that you never knew about and you just think well how useful is that for your essay writing, and using Master Documents instead of writing a big old long essay out and splitting it up into chapters and – so you don’t have your whole document saved in one big file, you’ve got all these little chapters that are then imported in and Word does that for you. No one’s told me that before. And I’ve been on an Excel course since I’ve been here and I’ve just – I thought I knew how to use Excel, of course you do, you’ve come from university, ah university student, I know a lot of stuff, but geez, no. 

Interviewer:	They seem really simple when you’re just using them to begin with and actually they can do all this really complicated stuff.

Subject:	And it’s not even that hard to get it to do the complicated stuff either. And just learning, yes, software packages really.

Interviewer:	So, do you think what you’ve learnt here will help you when you go back to uni?

Subject:	Definitely, definitely. It was an experience worth having and I’ve still got a couple of months left.

Interviewer:	Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

Subject:	Yeah, um, we had, um, I think it was a… Well, we had – we had, um, because we do mechanical engineering and they go down, um, we do a machining, um, module where we have to go into the workshop and wear steel-toe-cap boots and don’t chop off fingers and stuff like that. And we had, um – as soon as you start in mechanical engineering they tell you about wearing white coats and steel-toe-caps and all this kind of stuff, so we’ve kind of had that.

Interviewer:	Did you have to do health and safety training when you got here as well?

Subject:	No. There wasn’t any training. There is a – you get inducted, so they tell you what you need to do, where – where all the facilities are and all that kind of stuff. If you work in a particular area then you then get safety training, like I – I worked down in, um, the test rig downstairs and I got told all about how to use that rig and, um – and when you get to told how to use the rig they also tell you about health and safety with that rig. But I mean there’s no point me learning about what to do on the shop floor if I'm not working on the shop floor and I never go down there, so…

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think there’s anything else the university could have done to help prepare you for coming on placement?

Subject:	I don’t know. I think that’s the point of coming on placement, to learn how it is in industry. Academia is very different to the real world, very much so. It was a big shock coming from [university] where you’re told it’s a certain, you know exactly what you’re products are.
You know exactly what you want, what you’re told to do. You have a project, you have a deadline, you’re told what you have to do by when and, you know, your given your group and everything. It’s just not like that in the workplace, and coming here and having my work rate shrink was just – I was sitting there going, all right, I’ve done this work really quickly, come on, give me something else to do and it’s like well no, you know. And it was probably that I hadn’t done it properly or something like that, but I thought I’d done it properly and one thing my boss pointed out was – I was given, um, a project in – at the beginning of the my placement, so 21st of June, and that project’s still going on now, which tells you the depth and scale of this project, and my first reaction was right, solve this project, two weeks, you know. Get a solution, find a solution, do it and then it’s done. It’s not like that, it’s a gradual process. It’s finding out this, finding out that, see how people react to this and blah di blah. That was a big shock, having to do that, because everything was so much – the – looking into the future is looking three weeks ahead, not looking five years, as it is in a company.

Interviewer:	So do you think that university and work have got different goals and priorities?

Subject:	Yes. I mean I appreciate, well yeah, I mean they must do. They’ve got targets to set, they’ve got exams to set, I don’t get tested here, you know. If I don’t do the work, someone’s on my back about it, or I get help because I’ve not been able to do it. In university, I you can’t do something, usually your lecturers aren’t about so you just find your own way of doing it, but here there’s actually help, which is unusual also – so it’s a completely different way of working, so yes, completely different targets.

Interviewer:	Did it take a while getting used to…

Subject:	Yeah. I was sat twiddling my thumbs for ages, because when I came here and they thought I was coming in a different week or something like that and it so happened that the – my supervisor was away on business in a different country somewhere, so I was sat here and I got taken down to the shop floor to do like it’s – it’s, um, like work on all the machines and everything, which is not – I mean there’s one reason to do a degree now, which is so I don’t end up there, basically, you know, I didn’t enjoy it.

Interviewer:	You know what you don’t want to do?

Subject:	I know what I don’t want to do. I didn’t enjoy it and I was just – it was important that I found out how these things work for the company, I think. So I was stuck doing that and then I got given about two projects and for me I was used to having more. I’m used to a faster pace of life, I suppose. Considering I started on 21st of June and my exams had finished about two weeks earlier, so my brain was racing and it was – it was up for it, you know, it wanted something really difficult, something really challenging, but as it happens I’m only starting to get challenging work sort of now, before that it was all background and let’s see what she can do and things like that. It’s so much slower.

Interviewer:	Was it difficult getting into working nine til five and that sort of thing?

Subject:	No, because mechanical engineering is nine til five anyway, practically. Um, you get coffee breaks here, not much difference. I’ve done jobs – I’ve worked jobs before. I’ve worked nine to five before, so…

Interviewer:	Okay. Are you looking forward to going back to uni?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Why not?

Subject:	Because – because I know what’s waiting for me. I know – I know how much harder the course is going to get. I know exactly what I'm going to be doing. I know I’m going to be staying up til three o’clock in the morning doing crazy amounts of work and sort of running around trying to get from lecture to lecture and being challenged and completely not knowing what I’m doing. Whereas here, it’s a bit more, you know, you get told what you’re doing in a way. I mean it’s all about finding your own way in the workplace, but I don’t know, like… it’s difficult to explain. In some respects the university tells you exactly what you’re supposed to be doing and yet they leave you alone to do it, whereas at work you don’t get told what you’re doing but you have help to help you understand –

Interviewer:	There’s more support and guidance in a way?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer that sort of…

Subject:	I don’t know. I think they both have merit. I mean there’s been times at work when I’ve been absolutely miserable and just completely lost all motivation and just sat there and not done any work at all for maybe a whole day and just surfed the internet or something and no one says anything. No one comes up to you and says, ‘What the hell are you doing?’ you know, ‘Do some work’. It’s like no one notices, so it’s all up to you; it’s all self-motivation and to some degree, university requires a lot more discipline because you have tutorials to be in by dates, such and such, you have this project to be in by date such and such. I mean if you don’t do it, no one’s going to come and hit you on the head, but if you don’t do it you know you’re going to fail your degree, so there’s a bit of cause and reaction there.

Interviewer:	So it’s different types of pressure?

Subject:	Yeah, very much so.

Interviewer:	Okay, how many women does [company] employ do you think?

Subject:	In D&D there’s currently three including me.

Interviewer:	Out of about how many people?

Subject:	Um, there’s about approximately, in – I only know in Design and Development. In Design and Development it’s sort of 35, 40 people.

Interviewer:	So it’s definitely male-dominated.

Subject:	Yeah, and the women that are here, they do, um, it’s engineering-specific clerical work, basically, because you’re taking technical drawings and you have to, um, work with them and see what materials are used and keep the systems up to date. I'm not entirely sure their exact job, but it’s not as mundane as clerical work, but it’s basically you need a little bit of engineering knowledge, but you don’t need –

Interviewer:	But they’re not engineers.

Subject:	No, they’re not, no.

Interviewer:	Okay, do the company have a structure or programme in place for you to follow as a placement student?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be a good idea if they did?

Subject:	Um, I don’t know, because I don’t think you can in this business. For the Design and Development the projects are always changing. Um, the guide that we’ve been using whilst I’ve been here, or my boss has been using, is, um, the one given by the IMechE and the DIS qualification that you get at the end of this year out, which is really explicit and really helpful. I think as long as you’re following that, um, you don’t really need anything else. But having said that, I've never experienced one where there has been. I mean I suppose if you had a structured programme then there wouldn’t be these times of a lull in your work, because it would be more organised, but no one knows what they’re going to be doing from one day to the next in this place.

Interviewer:	Do you have appraisals with your boss or anything like that?

Subject:	No, not – not as part of the – as part of the company. Um, I'm required to have three visits a year from my tutor as a part of the DIS placement scheme.

Interviewer:	How many times have they been to visit you?

Subject:	He’s been once and he’s going to be coming again at the end of this month and then he’ll come again, um, just before I leave. So, sort of May time.

Interviewer:	Good. Did you know the person that came to visit you?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Would it have been more helpful if it was someone that you knew, do you think?

Subject:	Um, I don’t know. It would have been nice to see someone I knew, but at the end of the day, I’ll talk to anyone me. It’s not a big issue.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s important that a supervisor from uni does come to visit you?

Subject:	Yeah, because I think if you’ve been put in a bad position and you didn’t have anyone to come and see you then you’d be in trouble. I mean as it was I was okay, but I mean someone else might not have been.

Interviewer:	Do they speak to your manager as well?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, well he’s actually, um, doing some work for Loughborough University. He’s done some research for [company]. It’s the managing – the – the – D&D, Design and Development director, which is why I struggled so much with that, the Design and Development director actually knows, um, one of the head, um, lecturers at Loughborough in, um, mechanical engineering department. So they went to like [university] together and so, um, they talk to each other and he’s seconded some work out to them to help the research and stuff.

Interviewer:	Okay. Would you be happy to go to the placement tutor then if you did have any problems, or would you go to someone else?

Subject:	I’d more likely bring it up in work and talk to my supervisor about it, or talk to someone here that could help me, than go to him, because I think I could sort it out myself. I don’t think he’s kind of there for that. I think he’s there if you have some seriously big problems, then I’d probably go to him if I didn’t feel comfortable about going to them at work.

Interviewer:	Okay, do you feel like the company have given you an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	No. No, I… I got pretty down about a couple of weeks ago. I don’t know if it’s the weather, but I was just stuck with what I call monkey work. It’s not interesting, it’s inputting into computer data basically and I mean it’s – it’s not as bad as all that. It’s a project I’m working on and I know what I’m doing and all this kind of stuff. It’s just – I was just really, really annoyed. I mean Design and Development has times like that. I mean if you get a meter, a competitor’s meter from a different company and you’re building a meter which is supposed to do the same function, then you need to test the competitor’s meter. So I was doing that and that took me about six months to do that and basically all it is, is this meter goes into the water and you get a pipe running through it, you have like a – a display machinery next to it and you press the Start button then the water flows through and the tank fills up and when it stops you say right, we need to drain the tanks then, and you press the Drain button. And this goes on, because you need to – there are about a 14-point test, some of which, depending on which flow rate you're going at, the test can take like three hours, because like the lowest flow rate is three hours. So it goes from like ten minutes to three hours, and then – so there’s many points along there, and then, er, you’ve got to do that ten times, and it’s just dear God, I just can’t do this, I'm going to go insane, I really am. So I mean there was that and with the computer inputting data were my two projects at the time that I could get on with and it was just too much. Anyway, it just so happens that this week you’ve caught me on the hop because one of the actual, um, contractors, design engineers, has gone off sick, he’s got a chest infection, so I’ve been dumped with his work and I’ve never done anything like it in my life. Oh my God, it’s proper work for once, and I think this is the first time I’ve actually been given any proper work, apart from the sort of – for the projects. I mean I’ve been around the company and I’ve done lots of different things and if I wrote down exactly what I did you’d look at it and you’d think oh, you know, she’s actually done something. But at the time, because it moves so slowly, you kind of don’t feel like you’re doing very much at all.

Interviewer:	So do you feel you’ve been treated like the student then, or…?

Subject:	Very much so, but at the same time, this is the stuff that’s going into production now. I can fully understand why you wouldn’t want to give a student the responsibility for something which could cost the company millions. It could send this company down the toilet if you do it wrong. I mean for a bit of tooling you could charge like about £10,000 for a bit of tooling and if you’ve done the drawing wrong and you’ve not dimensioned it correctly, or maybe you took too long doing the drawing and then you missed the deadline, it could set the project back by I don’t know how many months, just because the manufacturer can’t do the tooling then because he’s got another job on or something like that.

Interviewer:	That’s quite scary.

Subject:	It is, it is a lot of responsibility, if you get out there. Like where I am at the minute with this guy’s work, he’s off sick, I’ve got given his work and I have to get this drawing done and I have no idea how to do it, so everyone’s having to help me out because I just don’t know. But I mean once I do one it will be easier to do the next one and so on. It’s a good opportunity; I’m glad he went off sick. I'm glad he’s ill.

Interviewer:	You like a challenge then.

Subject:	I do, yeah.

Interviewer:	So, have you spoken to anyone about the type of work that you’re doing and maybe asked for more responsibility or do you not think that’s …

Subject:	I – I got annoyed last year and I – I didn’t say I wanted more responsibility, what I said was, you know, ‘I’m running out of work, can I have some more work to do?’ and I got given some more testing, which really wasn’t what I had in mind. And then I got bored with that and asked again, to get motivated, ‘Can I have some more work to do?’ so I got given, um, quite a nice project, I thought. So, off I went, talked to everyone and it turns out yes it is quite a nice project, kind of, except it involves even more testing. Oh for goodness sake, I’m just sick of doing testing, honestly. At the moment – I got – I got kind of disheartened and I didn’t do any work for a couple of weeks and, of course, no one notices, okay, and then I got – I turned around to myself and go, ‘No, no, no, come on, this is – this is what you’re here for, you’ve got to make it what you want it to be, it’s not going to happen just by sitting back. You’ve got to make it what you want it to be’. So I thought right, well I’ll just do all the work they’ve given me and then I’ll, um, I’ll go to him and I’ll say, ‘Right, I’ve got no work and this time I want some decent work’ and I’ll say what kind of thing I want. But and then I started doing this work and it’s just taking me ages to finish it so… Okay, by the end of this month I will have it done and then – and then I shall go in and talk to him again.

Interviewer:	Is your boss – do you find him approachable?

Subject:	Very much so, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given enough support as a placement student or as a new recruit for the company?

Subject:	Um, support, what do you mean by support?

Interviewer:	I suppose, they’ve given you the work but do you think they let you find your own feet or have they been checking things with you or that you’re ok all the time, or have they given you space for you to go to them if you need help and stuff like that?

Subject:	The way it works is I get given a project by my – by my big boss man, as I call him, and he says, ‘This is what I want you to do’ and it’s usually a bit hazy and usually a bit kind of like, ‘Well, you know, I want something like this, but not’ so I go away and I say, ‘Okay’ and so I usually just do what he says and then about a week later we’ll have another meeting and I’ll say, ‘Well this is what I’ve done; what do you think?’ ‘That’s nice. I’ve been thinking, let’s do it this way instead’ and it just kind of rolls on like that as opposed to anything else. If I get stuck doing what I'm doing, I’ve got people to help me. I’ve been assigned a mentor here …

Interviewer:	What do you think about the idea of mentoring? Do you think it’s a good idea?

Subject:	Um, I think my mentor here feels a bit lost really, because I’ve got big boss man and a mentor and the idea was when I first came here was that my mentor would be giving me work to do and he would help me out. But the way it’s worked out is that the big boss man gives me my work and I talk mainly to him. If I have an odd little problem about something or I'm not understanding something, maybe even just about finding a drawing or something like that, I go to my mentor. I quite like that arrangement, which is – I think it’s a rare opportunity that you’ll get to talk to someone with as much experience as my big boss man. I mean he is the director of Design and Development. He’s worked in [company], he’s worked with [company], he’s worked with quite a few companies. He is s managerial director. He studied mechanical engineering, got a Master’s at [university]. I mean it’s kind of like where my career path could be going is kind of where he is at the minute, so it’s interesting just how much –

Interviewer:	He’s more like a role model?

Subject:	Kind of, yes. He is – he would be a very good role model, definitely. I definitely do look at him and think well, you know, I like the way he does things. I like the way he talks to people and I like the way he doesn’t take things – he doesn’t appear to take things so seriously all the time, you know. If he’s telling someone to do work he’ll have a bit of a joke with them about it. He’ll say, ‘You know, we need this done, but you know it’s quite funny how I’ve got into this position isn’t it…’ and things like that. I like that about him, definitely.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you do treat him as a mentor even though he’s not your official mentor?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, I guess I do, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Is there anyone else that you go to for advice and stuff, not necessarily about how to do work but just like you were saying earlier you’re sometimes nervous about presentations or something like that?

Subject:	There’s two people. I’ve got my big boss manager who gives me all my work, I never go to him for advice, ever. I ask him about – sometimes about where he’s come from and stuff like that, because it’s interesting. Um, for advice on things, I’ll come to him with problems like technical – to my big boss man with problems and he’ll probably give me a solution. For other things I go to my mentor or to the guy who sits opposite me. It’s like, yeah, there’s a wealth of knowledge there and I’m like oh, you know, I don’t know what I'm doing, I’ve not even a clue and it’s like, ‘Well, have you gone and asked such and such?’ like ‘Who are they?’. ‘Well, you know, they sit at the bottom and that’s their subject’. ‘Oh, okay’ and things like that. I mean you wouldn't know who to talk to unless there was someone to tell you who to talk to really. I mean even silly things like ‘oh, where do I get the paperclips from?’

Interviewer:	Are you in touch with other people on placement off your course?

Subject:	Yes, yes I am, yeah.

Interviewer:	Has that been a helpful sharing experiences or anything?

Subject:	I think everyone – everyone is as bored as I am. Not that I'm bored, but it’s working, it’s not… we do have the lulls, I think, depending on what kind of personality you are depends on what you focus on. Everyone I’ve spoken to who’s been on placement has said they’d been bored out of their tree.

Interviewer:	Okay. Are there any other students on placement here at all?

Subject:	No, no, no. They’ve got apprentices, which have sort of come out of school and they train them up and they put them on BTec courses and eventually sometimes they go on to do a degree course.

Interviewer:	Do you have to do lots of group work?

Subject:	No, I don’t do any group work at all. Despite being told at university, ‘Well, you know, you’re always going to do group work.’

Interviewer:	Now that you’ve been in work, do you think doing group work at university is useful?

Subject:	No. I think, I was speaking to a lecturer about this the other day and, you know, I think it’s useful to a point, but I think in fact it’s got a bit OTT at the minute, especially in mech eng. Projects that aren’t supposed to be, um, group work have been turned into group work purely to do with the fact that the lecturer has run out of time and if he puts people into groups then that’s a factor of five less that he doesn’t have to mark, or something like that, you know? And I think that has a lot of bearing on how they do it, because from my experience I don’t think anyone works in a group here. Um, I mean you have project teams, but the way it works is you have, um, a leader and the leader sort of gives the work out.

Interviewer:	So you’re all assigned specific roles?

Subject:	Exactly so you don’t need to talk to anyone else, maybe to get a drawing, maybe to ask them something, but there’s nothing like the amount of group work you’ve got to do at university.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be better if group work at university was organised more like that?

Subject:	The thing that annoys me about group work at university is the fact that it is really, really haphazard about who you get put with and you can get put in a group with someone who doesn’t do any work and that automatically puts the onus on everyone else and your grades suffer because of it and that is really annoying. Um, if it was in industry then that person would get fired and I don’t – I don’t see the point really.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s fine. How would you summarise your placement so far then?

Subject:	It’s been an experience.

Interviewer:	A good one?

Subject:	I think all experiences are good. I can’t say there’s anything that I’ve ever done that hasn’t taught me something.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement, or do you think everything about it’s beneficial?

Subject:	I would like to be given more responsibility at some point earlier than I have been given it. I mean like I said, it’s only – I mean how many months have I been here now? Eight – eight and a half I think and it’s only about two days ago that I’ve been given an actual D&D project and that’s only happened because someone’s gone off sick. Other than that, I’ve been passed off with what I call monkey work again. Sometimes I’ve been given stuff, but it’s more like sort of assembling data from various people, which is good on the people skills, though, of course. So, kind of more responsibility would have been nice.

Interviewer:	I guess that’s what you would say has been the worst thing about the placement?

Subject:	I personally, I like challenges. I might scream when I see them, but once I’ve done them I get – I do appreciate them very much so and a lot of the time I don’t feel particularly challenged intellectually. I mean I know there’s a time constraint but I’ve never actually had to use my brain. I mean I had a resit in the summer and that was like the first time I’d ever done anything that was remotely what I’d call using my brain and I was – I was excited, oh fantastic, do some revision, whoo-hoo, use my brain, fantastic. I mean it just felt so good and it’s like well it shouldn’t be like that, surely? Really shouldn’t be.

Interviewer:	What would you say has been the best thing about the placement then?

Subject:	I’d say getting – gathering a large amount of information on how to do things in a more efficient way, I’d say. Like with all the software that I'm learning and the courses that I’ve been going on. I’ve been on an Excel course and I’ve been on, um, Microsoft Project. University doesn’t teach you about Microsoft Project, they just say, ‘You need to produce a Gant chart, use Microsoft Project’, they don’t tell you how to use it, which I thought was quite annoying as well, but I’ve actually been taught this time. I've been on a course with everyone else.

Interviewer:	They’ve sent you on quite a few training things?

Subject:	There was, I think it’s three I've been on and I’ve got another one coming up. I’ve done, um, an Excel, um, beginners, which is kind of really, really easy because I’ve used it, but there were a few little things that were quite nice to learn. Um, been on a business process management, which is all to do with gate systems and things like that and how to manage projects and how to make sure they progress and find out which ones are the duds and get rid of them and progress on with the ones that have more potential and such and such, blah di blah di blah, it goes on. And, um, I’ve been on to a beginner’s Microsoft Project one and I will be going on to do, um, a higher one – a higher Microsoft Project one, advanced.

Interviewer:	That’s quite good. Do you think that the placement experience has changed you personally?

Subject:	Yeah. I’m certainly more confident, talk to people a lot more now. I can, um – I can, um, read between the lines a bit more I think. I'm not as – I don’t accept things as face value as much any more. I sort of think well what are they actually trying to say and, you know, or I know what you’re up to, type thing. Don’t even try it with me, I could see you coming a mile away, mate.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Yes, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s fine. We put that in because some people are working on construction sites and things and don’t always have women’s toilets, but going back to the gender things, can you think of any occasions where you think that the fact that you’re a woman has determined reactions that you’ve got from people?

Subject:	Um, I think I, er, I milk it sometimes, which is probably not the best thing to do in terms of, they’re probably quite open minded to begin with, but the way I act they probably think well, she’s just a typical girl. In terms of going down on the test rigs, a lot of the time there is some really – some heavy equipment about, some – when a pipe’s been pressurised and I’ve got to open it, the handle to open it’s really stiff because it’s all pressurised and I can’t actually move it because I'm not strong enough so I have to get one of the guys to do it or something. And carrying these meters which are just like lumps of iron, they are like literally castings of iron, carrying them down and doing this kind of stuff it’s – I need help with that sort of thing. Sometimes I sort of play up to being a bit ditzy so I can get a bit more help and if you play up to being ditzy then they don’t actually mind doing the help so much. I think – I don’t know how much – I get a lot of help here but I don’t know how much a guy would get. I don’t know how much they would be told to get on with it and stop being such a girl.

Interviewer:	So you think it’s maybe worked to your advantage more than a disadvantage?

Subject:	Yeah. I mean there’s certainly – sometimes, I don’t know whether it’s – you see it’s difficult to say whether it’s because I’m a student or whether it’s because I’m a girl that people will turn round and say things, but I mean, um, like I'll go down and I’ll go ask someone down in sales some sort of questions about something and they’ll try to fob me off with answers that aren’t relevant and I’ve turned round to one guy and it’s like, ‘Well, you know what, that’s not what I asked you for? Have you not got anything like this?’ and he was like, ‘Damn, I wish – I’d hoped you hadn’t noticed’. It’s like, what? Do I have to always be on my toes just in case someone’s telling me rubbish.

Interviewer:	Have they had placement students before?

Subject:	Apparently they have, yeah. Apparently they have. Um, I think the last placement student they had was about three years ago, so it’s been a while since they’ve had them but apparently they did have them.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you still think that you want a career in engineering?

Subject:	Not so much, not so much, um… I don’t know –

Interviewer:	Is that because this experience has put you off or…?

Subject:	It has. It has in some respects, I think, just because I, um, it’s not how – I'm undecided. I probably – I like – the whole reason why I chose engineering – one of the reasons why I chose engineering was it was quite nice to do a degree and then be able to just go into a job that was actually to do with the degree, instead of doing Business and not really knowing where you’ll end up with something like that. And – so I always imagined myself doing engineering. I really don’t know what I’d do if I didn’t do engineering because it’s been in my head for that long. Coming out of this placement, it’s a lot – there’s a lot less engineering in it than I thought there would be, but I think – I think the way it would work is I would actually stay in engineering but go into a business role, because I think that you do need the engineering knowledge for some jobs, but you can sort of not do any of the technical stuff.

Interviewer:	If you stay in engineering do you think you’ll go for a more managerial route?

Subject:	I think so. I don’t know. Um, might change my mind in a month or so, I suppose. 

Interviewer:	If they offered you a job here when you finished would you come back?

Subject:	No. No. One I've not had the best time here that I’ve… I mean on the one hand if I write it all down like I said, it would look like I’ve done a lot, but in terms of how I feel about the place it’s just – it doesn’t push me enough, it doesn’t challenge me enough and also I think it’s important in the early stages of your career to go around and see what kind of industries there are instead of settling for the first thing that’s given to you. So, I wouldn’t… but having said that, if I didn’t get a job anywhere else I’d have to because I need the money, so…

Interviewer:	Would you recommend someone else to do a placement here then?

Subject:	No. No. No, I wouldn’t. If they’re anything like me they’ll want to be challenged and this place just doesn’t push you enough. I don’t think I’ve ever been in a position where I’ve actually sat down and gone oh my God, I’ve got this deadline here, I’ve got that deadline there, there’s no way I’m every going to be finished and then actually got through to it and done it. It’s been more like ah, I’ve got four weeks to do that, I can just sit here and do nothing for five days and then I can do that work in a day. More like that kind of thing, especially when you know you’re not going to be checked up on.

Interviewer:	My first job was a bit like that. I had two weeks off sick or something and I came back, nobody had been doing my job but it wasn’t like I had to catch up on stuff. It’s like nobody’s missed you.

Subject:	Exactly. Yeah, you do feel like that and I think I don’t feel particularly valued at all. I feel like Sunday and Sunday night when I’m up visiting friends or something like that, I think well, you know what, I won’t go into work tomorrow because you know what, no one will notice and if they did notice, the only reason why they would notice is because my clocking in card hasn’t been used. And I think that’s a sad position to be in. A very sad position to be in and that’s what depresses me so much about this place, is the fact that no one would notice, no-one does care, so.

Interviewer:	But despite all that, do you think that that experience will help you when you start work after uni?

Subject:	Oh of course, yes. If nothing, because my CV will have that on it. I don’t have to tell them the truth about what I’ve been doing; I can big it up and say yeah! 

Interviewer:	And you’ve got all the training and things that you’ve done and that to put on your CV.

Subject:	Yeah, definitely, yeah. I mean that kind of stuff is stuff that I should know already, apart from the business process thing’s good anyway, but the Excel, yes I can put it on there but it’s kind of like well everyone knows Excel now, do you know what I mean? Microsoft Project is probably quite nice, especially if I’ve done the advanced one by then. Yeah, I’m going to push the thing and get out of it what I want, I think. I think I – I gave up for about four or five months and just decided well I’m just going to sit here and let things take over me and that didn’t work out so well, so I’ve changed tactics now.

Interviewer:	How did you find moving down here?

Subject:	Oh, it’s got easier, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Did you know anyone here?

Subject:	No, didn’t know anyone here. Um, I found loads of houses on the internet, came down one day in the middle of my exams, which was quite annoying, and walked around the whole of [town] because the bus timetable, there wasn’t one and [town] is a dump, so just walked round – luckily it wasn’t raining – and walked to all these places and found a nice house and said, ‘Right, I’ll take it’ and then I moved in. It was as easy as that.

Interviewer:	Have you actually worked for your – the DIS?

Subject:	Have I done any work? Yeah.

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you have to do?

Subject:	I have to produce a 5,000-word mini dissertation on a topic which has been decided between me and my, um, big boss man and I’ve got a title, I’ve just got to do it. (Okay) Yeah. It’s not a very exciting title, but… 

Interviewer:	And is that just like a pass or fail type of thing?

Subject:	It is, yeah, pass or fail.

Interviewer:	Okay, these are the last questions now and they’re things that I asked you last time. It’s not a test, to see if you get the same answer, it’s just to see if your opinion has changed since your new experiences. So what five words would you used to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry and your experience of the engineering industry?

Subject:	The engineering industry, um… haphazard, in the way that it just – nothing ever goes to plan and you just have to muddle around and try and get the best out of it you can. Um, what else? Difficult, definitely, and complex, um… there’s not a word that can describe it, but I’d say sort of communication in terms of you need a lot of it, you know, to be able to communicate a lot and not in the way that I originally thought you’d have to, like for drawings and things, it’s more about talking and explaining and –

Interviewer:	Do you have to do a lot of work explaining the engineering stuff to people that aren’t engineers or…?

Subject:	No, it’s mainly – it’s mainly engineer to engineer here. I don’t think I've ever had to explain anything to a non-engineer. It’s getting used to the jargon that they use here, you know, like, ‘Ah, that’s a 50-mili bore such and such. Why are you using a road tool which is only 20-mili with a circumferential something or other or such and blah di blah’, you know. I mean it’s just ‘What?’ (inaudible) or a PCND or something, I don’t know, all this stuff they just come out with, they just (inaudible) I suppose if you’re in this industry it’s fine, but yeah. I think I’ve got one more word to think of, um… one more word about engineering… don’t know… varied, most definitely varied. It’s not all about technical, it’s not all about drawing, it’s not all about managerial, it’s not all about marketing, which I didn’t even think it was about marketing before, but it is.

Interviewer:	Bit of everything.

Subject:	Yeah, cost, materials, everything. And I think –

Interviewer:	Did you do any business type modules at uni?

Subject:	Yeah, we did, um – yeah, we did, but it’s like we did, um, we did both business, quality and law, so it was like a double module with those three subjects in it – oh sorry, business law, quality and something or other, I forget. But there was this whole thing about manufacturing processes are supposed to conform to ISO standards and all this kind of stuff and they actually do that here, so it’s been interesting to see that being implemented. Um, and I did get a brief look into it in that I did have, um, that business process, um, management course I went on dealt with the same sort of things that I’ve been taught at uni, which was – but more concentrated on this business and it made a lot more sense. So, definitely varied. And I think as a person I’d rather be an all rounder instead of a design technician or a manufacturing person. I’d rather be able to sit there and be able to dabble.

Interviewer:	You’d rather be a generalist than a specialist.

Subject:	Indeed, indeed. 

Interviewer:	Okay, we spoke a bit earlier about advantages, but do you think that there are any other advantages or any disadvantages now to being a woman in a male dominated…

Subject:	Yeah, God like if you want to look nice and you wear like heels and the floor here, man they can here you coming a mile away, it’s just like (makes sound). So that’s quite bad. Um, in terms of, I don’t know, I don’t think so. Everyone – I think it’s the kind of workplace this is and the only reason why you’d stay here permanently for the rest of your life is probably one of those because of the people jobbies as opposed to you love the job so much, it’s going to be all the people here are really nice. Um, I don’t – I mean I might just be being completely blind here and not seeing that people are being sexist or something, but I’ve never experienced that.

Interviewer:	Why then do you think that there maybe aren’t more women here?

Subject:	I know it sounds a bit clichéd when they say that girls can’t think like guys, but it’s really true. It’s like there are certain things that I’ve found here that I’ve found a lot more difficult than other people and there are certain things I’m a lot better at. I’m a lot better at organising information, um, collecting information and all this kind of stuff, but as soon as you give me, um, give me something to, um, like find the solution to or like imagine you’re in a different sort of orientation or something, it takes a lot more brain power to do that. I can do it, it’s not that I can’t do it, I can do it, but it takes me a wee bit longer than perhaps someone else in the company and you know, that might just be because they’ve been here longer. There’s lots of things it might be, but I think something that I struggle with is thinking in a different way. Thinking out of the box, as they say.

Interviewer:	Do you think it matters then that there aren’t more women in engineering?

Subject:	Yes, because I think the only reason why I find that difficult is because that’s the way this industry is set up to think as and I think that there may be another way of doing that may appeal to women. I think if you gave a woman the same job as a man she’d go about it in a completely different way.

Interviewer:	But she’d still get it done?

Subject:	Yes and it mightn’t be that one was better than the other, it would just be different, so…

Interviewer:	Have you got any ideas now about how more women could be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Um, I think it’s just getting it into schools and showing people, giving actual real examples and then having women go to schools and sort of say, ‘Well, you know what? I did this. It was a little bit hard, but look at the advantages I'm getting out of it.’ Showing the rewards that you can get from putting a bit more effort in, because I think for me to do – to do a job like a business job or a law job is a lot easier than doing an engineering job and all you need to do is make one more attractive than the other. Take the easy road or take the slightly harder road and get more benefits out of it. I think I can do the work, it might take me a little bit longer, it might be a little bit harder for me, but I can still do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that business and law are portrayed to the public as being more glamorous?

Subject:	The law is. The law is because of all the TV shows. Um, business probably not so much. Business is the easy way out, but you see I find that if you do a subject like engineering you get a lot more respect from people. If you say, ‘I do law’ they go ‘Oh, you do law, great’. I mean and the big joke among the engineers at [university] is they’re doing Psychology. You know, you want to try a day doing our degree and see how you manage doing that, you know. We do this many hours and have this many exams and our course is so much harder than yours and – yeah, so I think it is, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s fantastic, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When did you start your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, 21st of June.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’ve been here ages now then, haven’t you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Nearly done.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They make water meters basically, um, for all different kinds of applications, some domestic, the kind of thing that you find outside your house, and some more industrial things that are for big power plants and that sort of thing, but only water at this company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it’s been really good. I think, um, you get some old timers that do treat you a bit differently, but I think that’s just because they’re older. Um, it’s quite amusing, I mean you’ve seen the number of doors there are here; everyone opens doors for me (inaudible) but I've certainly been treated with respect and what have you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, we’ll come back to that sort of stuff later. Most of the questions I’ve got are about how the placement’s going and how you think it relates to your course and stuff like that. So how useful do you think that your course has been to the work that you’re doing so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at all really it has to be said. Um, mainly the one thing that I’ve found useful from the course has been, um, the modelling that I’ve been doing, um, using computer packaging, but even that was so basic that I – as soon as I came here I was told, ‘Well, you know what, you can do it that way, but it’s not the best way to do it’ and you know, when you get into industry things are a bit more complicated and you have to really think more about what you’re doing and you don’t get these simple problems that you get at university; everything’s a lot more difficult and detailed and – because at the end of the day you’re going to be making tooling from this that’s got to make that product, so it has to be spot on and things from down to drawing etiquette and technique, we’re following British standards and to, um, just the technical ability to be able to model the sophistication of the parts, it’s just a bit extreme. But other than that I’ve not – not really use anything from my course. I’ve been mainly doing things, um, to do with the business management and project management and sort of brand awareness, so that’s more marketing and looking at that. So I’ve been doing – chopping and changing between all sorts of different things. (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything like the more generic skills from uni that you’ve used, like communication and organisation skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would say that they pale in comparison to the type of communication and, um, patience you need in a working environment. I’ve never met such a diverse amount of people and had to treat each one of them completely differently, because some people take things a little bit more seriously than others and some people, um, you have to be quite careful because if you don’t, I mean some people in here there’s a big joke, don’t go to this certain person because they will talk to you for hours and hours and hours and you’ve just got to be very tactful about the way you kind of say, ‘Well that’s nice, thank you for your information, but I really need to get on and do my work right now’. Things like that and doing presentations to the directors of the company and the directors of marketing and all this kind of stuff, it’s just nerve wracking and you don’t realise how much pressure gets put on you when you’re put in that sort of situation and you don’t know how you’ll cope until you actually do it. So it’s all about preparation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So is there anything that you wish you had learnt at uni before you came on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I wish that, um, there were several things that I found out here which would have made my life so much easier at university. Things – things, a lot about, um, mainly the software that – simple, little things, I can’t even – there are so many of them, even just using Word. I mean how much do you write on Word and there are all these different functions that you never knew about and you just think well how useful is that for your essay writing, and using Master Documents instead of writing a big old long essay out and splitting it up into chapters and – so you don’t have your whole document saved in one big file, you’ve got all these little chapters that are then imported in and Word does that for you. No one’s told me that before. And I’ve been on an Excel course since I’ve been here and I’ve just – I thought I knew how to use Excel, of course you do, you’ve come from university, ah university student, I know a lot of stuff, but geez, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: They seem really simple when you’re just using them to begin with and actually they can do all this really complicated stuff.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And it’s not even that hard to get it to do the complicated stuff either. And just learning, yes, software packages really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, do you think what you’ve learnt here will help you when you go back to uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, definitely. It was an experience worth having and I’ve still got a couple of months left.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, um, we had, um, I think it was a… Well, we had – we had, um, because we do mechanical engineering and they go down, um, we do a machining, um, module where we have to go into the workshop and wear steel-toe-cap boots and don’t chop off fingers and stuff like that. And we had, um – as soon as you start in mechanical engineering they tell you about wearing white coats and steel-toe-caps and all this kind of stuff, so we’ve kind of had that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have to do health and safety training when you got here as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. There wasn’t any training. There is a – you get inducted, so they tell you what you need to do, where – where all the facilities are and all that kind of stuff. If you work in a particular area then you then get safety training, like I – I worked down in, um, the test rig downstairs and I got told all about how to use that rig and, um – and when you get to told how to use the rig they also tell you about health and safety with that rig. But I mean there’s no point me learning about what to do on the shop floor if I'm not working on the shop floor and I never go down there, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you think there’s anything else the university could have done to help prepare you for coming on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I think that’s the point of coming on placement, to learn how it is in industry. Academia is very different to the real world, very much so. It was a big shock coming from [university] where you’re told it’s a certain, you know exactly what you’re products are. You know exactly what you want, what you’re told to do. You have a project, you have a deadline, you’re told what you have to do by when and, you know, your given your group and everything. It’s just not like that in the workplace, and coming here and having my work rate shrink was just – I was sitting there going, all right, I’ve done this work really quickly, come on, give me something else to do and it’s like well no, you know. And it was probably that I hadn’t done it properly or something like that, but I thought I’d done it properly and one thing my boss pointed out was – I was given, um, a project in – at the beginning of the my placement, so 21st of June, and that project’s still going on now, which tells you the depth and scale of this project, and my first reaction was right, solve this project, two weeks, you know. Get a solution, find a solution, do it and then it’s done. It’s not like that, it’s a gradual process. It’s finding out this, finding out that, see how people react to this and blah di blah. That was a big shock, having to do that, because everything was so much – the – looking into the future is looking three weeks ahead, not looking five years, as it is in a company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that university and work have got different goals and priorities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I mean I appreciate, well yeah, I mean they must do. They’ve got targets to set, they’ve got exams to set, I don’t get tested here, you know. If I don’t do the work, someone’s on my back about it, or I get help because I’ve not been able to do it. In university, I you can’t do something, usually your lecturers aren’t about so you just find your own way of doing it, but here there’s actually help, which is unusual also – so it’s a completely different way of working, so yes, completely different targets.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it take a while getting used to…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I was sat twiddling my thumbs for ages, because when I came here and they thought I was coming in a different week or something like that and it so happened that the – my supervisor was away on business in a different country somewhere, so I was sat here and I got taken down to the shop floor to do like it’s – it’s, um, like work on all the machines and everything, which is not – I mean there’s one reason to do a degree now, which is so I don’t end up there, basically, you know, I didn’t enjoy it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You know what you don’t want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I know what I don’t want to do. I didn’t enjoy it and I was just – it was important that I found out how these things work for the company, I think. So I was stuck doing that and then I got given about two projects and for me I was used to having more. I’m used to a faster pace of life, I suppose. Considering I started on 21st of June and my exams had finished about two weeks earlier, so my brain was racing and it was – it was up for it, you know, it wanted something really difficult, something really challenging, but as it happens I’m only starting to get challenging work sort of now, before that it was all background and let’s see what she can do and things like that. It’s so much slower.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it difficult getting into working nine til five and that sort of thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because mechanical engineering is nine til five anyway, practically. Um, you get coffee breaks here, not much difference. I’ve done jobs – I’ve worked jobs before. I’ve worked nine to five before, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are you looking forward to going back to uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because – because I know what’s waiting for me. I know – I know how much harder the course is going to get. I know exactly what I'm going to be doing. I know I’m going to be staying up til three o’clock in the morning doing crazy amounts of work and sort of running around trying to get from lecture to lecture and being challenged and completely not knowing what I’m doing. Whereas here, it’s a bit more, you know, you get told what you’re doing in a way. I mean it’s all about finding your own way in the workplace, but I don’t know, like… it’s difficult to explain. In some respects the university tells you exactly what you’re supposed to be doing and yet they leave you alone to do it, whereas at work you don’t get told what you’re doing but you have help to help you understand –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: There’s more support and guidance in a way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer that sort of…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I think they both have merit. I mean there’s been times at work when I’ve been absolutely miserable and just completely lost all motivation and just sat there and not done any work at all for maybe a whole day and just surfed the internet or something and no one says anything. No one comes up to you and says, ‘What the hell are you doing?’ you know, ‘Do some work’. It’s like no one notices, so it’s all up to you; it’s all self-motivation and to some degree, university requires a lot more discipline because you have tutorials to be in by dates, such and such, you have this project to be in by date such and such. I mean if you don’t do it, no one’s going to come and hit you on the head, but if you don’t do it you know you’re going to fail your degree, so there’s a bit of cause and reaction there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s different types of pressure?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, very much so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, how many women does [company] employ do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In D&D there’s currently three including me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Out of about how many people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, there’s about approximately, in – I only know in Design and Development. In Design and Development it’s sort of 35, 40 people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s definitely male-dominated.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and the women that are here, they do, um, it’s engineering-specific clerical work, basically, because you’re taking technical drawings and you have to, um, work with them and see what materials are used and keep the systems up to date. I'm not entirely sure their exact job, but it’s not as mundane as clerical work, but it’s basically you need a little bit of engineering knowledge, but you don’t need –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But they’re not engineers.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, they’re not, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do the company have a structure or programme in place for you to follow as a placement student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be a good idea if they did?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know, because I don’t think you can in this business. For the Design and Development the projects are always changing. Um, the guide that we’ve been using whilst I’ve been here, or my boss has been using, is, um, the one given by the IMechE and the DIS qualification that you get at the end of this year out, which is really explicit and really helpful. I think as long as you’re following that, um, you don’t really need anything else. But having said that, I've never experienced one where there has been. I mean I suppose if you had a structured programme then there wouldn’t be these times of a lull in your work, because it would be more organised, but no one knows what they’re going to be doing from one day to the next in this place.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have appraisals with your boss or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not – not as part of the – as part of the company. Um, I'm required to have three visits a year from my tutor as a part of the DIS placement scheme.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many times have they been to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s been once and he’s going to be coming again at the end of this month and then he’ll come again, um, just before I leave. So, sort of May time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Did you know the person that came to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would it have been more helpful if it was someone that you knew, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know. It would have been nice to see someone I knew, but at the end of the day, I’ll talk to anyone me. It’s not a big issue.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s important that a supervisor from uni does come to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because I think if you’ve been put in a bad position and you didn’t have anyone to come and see you then you’d be in trouble. I mean as it was I was okay, but I mean someone else might not have been.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do they speak to your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, well he’s actually, um, doing some work for Loughborough University. He’s done some research for [company]. It’s the managing – the – the – D&D, Design and Development director, which is why I struggled so much with that, the Design and Development director actually knows, um, one of the head, um, lecturers at Loughborough in, um, mechanical engineering department. So they went to like [university] together and so, um, they talk to each other and he’s seconded some work out to them to help the research and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Would you be happy to go to the placement tutor then if you did have any problems, or would you go to someone else?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d more likely bring it up in work and talk to my supervisor about it, or talk to someone here that could help me, than go to him, because I think I could sort it out myself. I don’t think he’s kind of there for that. I think he’s there if you have some seriously big problems, then I’d probably go to him if I didn’t feel comfortable about going to them at work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do you feel like the company have given you an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No, I… I got pretty down about a couple of weeks ago. I don’t know if it’s the weather, but I was just stuck with what I call monkey work. It’s not interesting, it’s inputting into computer data basically and I mean it’s – it’s not as bad as all that. It’s a project I’m working on and I know what I’m doing and all this kind of stuff. It’s just – I was just really, really annoyed. I mean Design and Development has times like that. I mean if you get a meter, a competitor’s meter from a different company and you’re building a meter which is supposed to do the same function, then you need to test the competitor’s meter. So I was doing that and that took me about six months to do that and basically all it is, is this meter goes into the water and you get a pipe running through it, you have like a – a display machinery next to it and you press the Start button then the water flows through and the tank fills up and when it stops you say right, we need to drain the tanks then, and you press the Drain button. And this goes on, because you need to – there are about a 14-point test, some of which, depending on which flow rate you're going at, the test can take like three hours, because like the lowest flow rate is three hours. So it goes from like ten minutes to three hours, and then – so there’s many points along there, and then, er, you’ve got to do that ten times, and it’s just dear God, I just can’t do this, I'm going to go insane, I really am. So I mean there was that and with the computer inputting data were my two projects at the time that I could get on with and it was just too much. Anyway, it just so happens that this week you’ve caught me on the hop because one of the actual, um, contractors, design engineers, has gone off sick, he’s got a chest infection, so I’ve been dumped with his work and I’ve never done anything like it in my life. Oh my God, it’s proper work for once, and I think this is the first time I’ve actually been given any proper work, apart from the sort of – for the projects. I mean I’ve been around the company and I’ve done lots of different things and if I wrote down exactly what I did you’d look at it and you’d think oh, you know, she’s actually done something. But at the time, because it moves so slowly, you kind of don’t feel like you’re doing very much at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you feel you’ve been treated like the student then, or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very much so, but at the same time, this is the stuff that’s going into production now. I can fully understand why you wouldn’t want to give a student the responsibility for something which could cost the company millions. It could send this company down the toilet if you do it wrong. I mean for a bit of tooling you could charge like about £10,000 for a bit of tooling and if you’ve done the drawing wrong and you’ve not dimensioned it correctly, or maybe you took too long doing the drawing and then you missed the deadline, it could set the project back by I don’t know how many months, just because the manufacturer can’t do the tooling then because he’s got another job on or something like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite scary.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is, it is a lot of responsibility, if you get out there. Like where I am at the minute with this guy’s work, he’s off sick, I’ve got given his work and I have to get this drawing done and I have no idea how to do it, so everyone’s having to help me out because I just don’t know. But I mean once I do one it will be easier to do the next one and so on. It’s a good opportunity; I’m glad he went off sick. I'm glad he’s ill.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You like a challenge then.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, have you spoken to anyone about the type of work that you’re doing and maybe asked for more responsibility or do you not think that’s …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I – I got annoyed last year and I – I didn’t say I wanted more responsibility, what I said was, you know, ‘I’m running out of work, can I have some more work to do?’ and I got given some more testing, which really wasn’t what I had in mind. And then I got bored with that and asked again, to get motivated, ‘Can I have some more work to do?’ so I got given, um, quite a nice project, I thought. So, off I went, talked to everyone and it turns out yes it is quite a nice project, kind of, except it involves even more testing. Oh for goodness sake, I’m just sick of doing testing, honestly. At the moment – I got – I got kind of disheartened and I didn’t do any work for a couple of weeks and, of course, no one notices, okay, and then I got – I turned around to myself and go, ‘No, no, no, come on, this is – this is what you’re here for, you’ve got to make it what you want it to be, it’s not going to happen just by sitting back. You’ve got to make it what you want it to be’. So I thought right, well I’ll just do all the work they’ve given me and then I’ll, um, I’ll go to him and I’ll say, ‘Right, I’ve got no work and this time I want some decent work’ and I’ll say what kind of thing I want. But and then I started doing this work and it’s just taking me ages to finish it so… Okay, by the end of this month I will have it done and then – and then I shall go in and talk to him again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is your boss – do you find him approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very much so, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given enough support as a placement student or as a new recruit for the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, support, what do you mean by support?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I suppose, they’ve given you the work but do you think they let you find your own feet or have they been checking things with you or that you’re ok all the time, or have they given you space for you to go to them if you need help and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The way it works is I get given a project by my – by my big boss man, as I call him, and he says, ‘This is what I want you to do’ and it’s usually a bit hazy and usually a bit kind of like, ‘Well, you know, I want something like this, but not’ so I go away and I say, ‘Okay’ and so I usually just do what he says and then about a week later we’ll have another meeting and I’ll say, ‘Well this is what I’ve done; what do you think?’ ‘That’s nice. I’ve been thinking, let’s do it this way instead’ and it just kind of rolls on like that as opposed to anything else. If I get stuck doing what I'm doing, I’ve got people to help me. I’ve been assigned a mentor here …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think about the idea of mentoring? Do you think it’s a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think my mentor here feels a bit lost really, because I’ve got big boss man and a mentor and the idea was when I first came here was that my mentor would be giving me work to do and he would help me out. But the way it’s worked out is that the big boss man gives me my work and I talk mainly to him. If I have an odd little problem about something or I'm not understanding something, maybe even just about finding a drawing or something like that, I go to my mentor. I quite like that arrangement, which is – I think it’s a rare opportunity that you’ll get to talk to someone with as much experience as my big boss man. I mean he is the director of Design and Development. He’s worked in [company], he’s worked with [company], he’s worked with quite a few companies. He is s managerial director. He studied mechanical engineering, got a Master’s at [university]. I mean it’s kind of like where my career path could be going is kind of where he is at the minute, so it’s interesting just how much –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: He’s more like a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Kind of, yes. He is – he would be a very good role model, definitely. I definitely do look at him and think well, you know, I like the way he does things. I like the way he talks to people and I like the way he doesn’t take things – he doesn’t appear to take things so seriously all the time, you know. If he’s telling someone to do work he’ll have a bit of a joke with them about it. He’ll say, ‘You know, we need this done, but you know it’s quite funny how I’ve got into this position isn’t it…’ and things like that. I like that about him, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that you do treat him as a mentor even though he’s not your official mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I guess I do, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone else that you go to for advice and stuff, not necessarily about how to do work but just like you were saying earlier you’re sometimes nervous about presentations or something like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s two people. I’ve got my big boss manager who gives me all my work, I never go to him for advice, ever. I ask him about – sometimes about where he’s come from and stuff like that, because it’s interesting. Um, for advice on things, I’ll come to him with problems like technical – to my big boss man with problems and he’ll probably give me a solution. For other things I go to my mentor or to the guy who sits opposite me. It’s like, yeah, there’s a wealth of knowledge there and I’m like oh, you know, I don’t know what I'm doing, I’ve not even a clue and it’s like, ‘Well, have you gone and asked such and such?’ like ‘Who are they?’. ‘Well, you know, they sit at the bottom and that’s their subject’. ‘Oh, okay’ and things like that. I mean you wouldn't know who to talk to unless there was someone to tell you who to talk to really. I mean even silly things like ‘oh, where do I get the paperclips from?’

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in touch with other people on placement off your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes I am, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that been a helpful sharing experiences or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think everyone – everyone is as bored as I am. Not that I'm bored, but it’s working, it’s not… we do have the lulls, I think, depending on what kind of personality you are depends on what you focus on. Everyone I’ve spoken to who’s been on placement has said they’d been bored out of their tree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are there any other students on placement here at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no, no. They’ve got apprentices, which have sort of come out of school and they train them up and they put them on BTec courses and eventually sometimes they go on to do a degree course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to do lots of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t do any group work at all. Despite being told at university, ‘Well, you know, you’re always going to do group work.’

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Now that you’ve been in work, do you think doing group work at university is useful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I think, I was speaking to a lecturer about this the other day and, you know, I think it’s useful to a point, but I think in fact it’s got a bit OTT at the minute, especially in mech eng. Projects that aren’t supposed to be, um, group work have been turned into group work purely to do with the fact that the lecturer has run out of time and if he puts people into groups then that’s a factor of five less that he doesn’t have to mark, or something like that, you know? And I think that has a lot of bearing on how they do it, because from my experience I don’t think anyone works in a group here. Um, I mean you have project teams, but the way it works is you have, um, a leader and the leader sort of gives the work out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re all assigned specific roles?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly so you don’t need to talk to anyone else, maybe to get a drawing, maybe to ask them something, but there’s nothing like the amount of group work you’ve got to do at university.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be better if group work at university was organised more like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The thing that annoys me about group work at university is the fact that it is really, really haphazard about who you get put with and you can get put in a group with someone who doesn’t do any work and that automatically puts the onus on everyone else and your grades suffer because of it and that is really annoying. Um, if it was in industry then that person would get fired and I don’t – I don’t see the point really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that’s fine. How would you summarise your placement so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s been an experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: A good one?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think all experiences are good. I can’t say there’s anything that I’ve ever done that hasn’t taught me something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement, or do you think everything about it’s beneficial?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would like to be given more responsibility at some point earlier than I have been given it. I mean like I said, it’s only – I mean how many months have I been here now? Eight – eight and a half I think and it’s only about two days ago that I’ve been given an actual D&D project and that’s only happened because someone’s gone off sick. Other than that, I’ve been passed off with what I call monkey work again. Sometimes I’ve been given stuff, but it’s more like sort of assembling data from various people, which is good on the people skills, though, of course. So, kind of more responsibility would have been nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I guess that’s what you would say has been the worst thing about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I personally, I like challenges. I might scream when I see them, but once I’ve done them I get – I do appreciate them very much so and a lot of the time I don’t feel particularly challenged intellectually. I mean I know there’s a time constraint but I’ve never actually had to use my brain.
