I mean I had a resit in the summer and that was like the first time I’d ever done anything that was remotely what I’d call using my brain and I was – I was excited, oh fantastic, do some revision, whoo-hoo, use my brain, fantastic. I mean it just felt so good and it’s like well it shouldn’t be like that, surely? Really shouldn’t be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say has been the best thing about the placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say getting – gathering a large amount of information on how to do things in a more efficient way, I’d say. Like with all the software that I'm learning and the courses that I’ve been going on. I’ve been on an Excel course and I’ve been on, um, Microsoft Project. University doesn’t teach you about Microsoft Project, they just say, ‘You need to produce a Gant chart, use Microsoft Project’, they don’t tell you how to use it, which I thought was quite annoying as well, but I’ve actually been taught this time. I've been on a course with everyone else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: They’ve sent you on quite a few training things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There was, I think it’s three I've been on and I’ve got another one coming up. I’ve done, um, an Excel, um, beginners, which is kind of really, really easy because I’ve used it, but there were a few little things that were quite nice to learn. Um, been on a business process management, which is all to do with gate systems and things like that and how to manage projects and how to make sure they progress and find out which ones are the duds and get rid of them and progress on with the ones that have more potential and such and such, blah di blah di blah, it goes on. And, um, I’ve been on to a beginner’s Microsoft Project one and I will be going on to do, um, a higher one – a higher Microsoft Project one, advanced.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite good. Do you think that the placement experience has changed you personally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I’m certainly more confident, talk to people a lot more now. I can, um – I can, um, read between the lines a bit more I think. I'm not as – I don’t accept things as face value as much any more. I sort of think well what are they actually trying to say and, you know, or I know what you’re up to, type thing. Don’t even try it with me, I could see you coming a mile away, mate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that’s fine. We put that in because some people are working on construction sites and things and don’t always have women’s toilets, but going back to the gender things, can you think of any occasions where you think that the fact that you’re a woman has determined reactions that you’ve got from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think I, er, I milk it sometimes, which is probably not the best thing to do in terms of, they’re probably quite open minded to begin with, but the way I act they probably think well, she’s just a typical girl. In terms of going down on the test rigs, a lot of the time there is some really – some heavy equipment about, some – when a pipe’s been pressurised and I’ve got to open it, the handle to open it’s really stiff because it’s all pressurised and I can’t actually move it because I'm not strong enough so I have to get one of the guys to do it or something. And carrying these meters which are just like lumps of iron, they are like literally castings of iron, carrying them down and doing this kind of stuff it’s – I need help with that sort of thing. Sometimes I sort of play up to being a bit ditzy so I can get a bit more help and if you play up to being ditzy then they don’t actually mind doing the help so much. I think – I don’t know how much – I get a lot of help here but I don’t know how much a guy would get. I don’t know how much they would be told to get on with it and stop being such a girl.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think it’s maybe worked to your advantage more than a disadvantage?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I mean there’s certainly – sometimes, I don’t know whether it’s – you see it’s difficult to say whether it’s because I’m a student or whether it’s because I’m a girl that people will turn round and say things, but I mean, um, like I'll go down and I’ll go ask someone down in sales some sort of questions about something and they’ll try to fob me off with answers that aren’t relevant and I’ve turned round to one guy and it’s like, ‘Well, you know what, that’s not what I asked you for? Have you not got anything like this?’ and he was like, ‘Damn, I wish – I’d hoped you hadn’t noticed’. It’s like, what? Do I have to always be on my toes just in case someone’s telling me rubbish.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have they had placement students before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Apparently they have, yeah. Apparently they have. Um, I think the last placement student they had was about three years ago, so it’s been a while since they’ve had them but apparently they did have them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you still think that you want a career in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not so much, not so much, um… I don’t know –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that because this experience has put you off or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It has. It has in some respects, I think, just because I, um, it’s not how – I'm undecided. I probably – I like – the whole reason why I chose engineering – one of the reasons why I chose engineering was it was quite nice to do a degree and then be able to just go into a job that was actually to do with the degree, instead of doing Business and not really knowing where you’ll end up with something like that. And – so I always imagined myself doing engineering. I really don’t know what I’d do if I didn’t do engineering because it’s been in my head for that long. Coming out of this placement, it’s a lot – there’s a lot less engineering in it than I thought there would be, but I think – I think the way it would work is I would actually stay in engineering but go into a business role, because I think that you do need the engineering knowledge for some jobs, but you can sort of not do any of the technical stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you stay in engineering do you think you’ll go for a more managerial route?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. I don’t know. Um, might change my mind in a month or so, I suppose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If they offered you a job here when you finished would you come back?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No. One I've not had the best time here that I’ve… I mean on the one hand if I write it all down like I said, it would look like I’ve done a lot, but in terms of how I feel about the place it’s just – it doesn’t push me enough, it doesn’t challenge me enough and also I think it’s important in the early stages of your career to go around and see what kind of industries there are instead of settling for the first thing that’s given to you. So, I wouldn’t… but having said that, if I didn’t get a job anywhere else I’d have to because I need the money, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend someone else to do a placement here then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. No. No, I wouldn’t. If they’re anything like me they’ll want to be challenged and this place just doesn’t push you enough. I don’t think I’ve ever been in a position where I’ve actually sat down and gone oh my God, I’ve got this deadline here, I’ve got that deadline there, there’s no way I’m every going to be finished and then actually got through to it and done it. It’s been more like ah, I’ve got four weeks to do that, I can just sit here and do nothing for five days and then I can do that work in a day. More like that kind of thing, especially when you know you’re not going to be checked up on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: My first job was a bit like that. I had two weeks off sick or something and I came back, nobody had been doing my job but it wasn’t like I had to catch up on stuff. It’s like nobody’s missed you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. Yeah, you do feel like that and I think I don’t feel particularly valued at all. I feel like Sunday and Sunday night when I’m up visiting friends or something like that, I think well, you know what, I won’t go into work tomorrow because you know what, no one will notice and if they did notice, the only reason why they would notice is because my clocking in card hasn’t been used. And I think that’s a sad position to be in. A very sad position to be in and that’s what depresses me so much about this place, is the fact that no one would notice, no-one does care, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But despite all that, do you think that that experience will help you when you start work after uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh of course, yes. If nothing, because my CV will have that on it. I don’t have to tell them the truth about what I’ve been doing; I can big it up and say yeah!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you’ve got all the training and things that you’ve done and that to put on your CV.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely, yeah. I mean that kind of stuff is stuff that I should know already, apart from the business process thing’s good anyway, but the Excel, yes I can put it on there but it’s kind of like well everyone knows Excel now, do you know what I mean? Microsoft Project is probably quite nice, especially if I’ve done the advanced one by then. Yeah, I’m going to push the thing and get out of it what I want, I think. I think I – I gave up for about four or five months and just decided well I’m just going to sit here and let things take over me and that didn’t work out so well, so I’ve changed tactics now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you find moving down here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, it’s got easier, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know anyone here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, didn’t know anyone here. Um, I found loads of houses on the internet, came down one day in the middle of my exams, which was quite annoying, and walked around the whole of [town] because the bus timetable, there wasn’t one and [town] is a dump, so just walked round – luckily it wasn’t raining – and walked to all these places and found a nice house and said, ‘Right, I’ll take it’ and then I moved in. It was as easy as that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you actually worked for your – the DIS?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Have I done any work? Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you have to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have to produce a 5,000-word mini dissertation on a topic which has been decided between me and my, um, big boss man and I’ve got a title, I’ve just got to do it. (Okay) Yeah. It’s not a very exciting title, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And is that just like a pass or fail type of thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is, yeah, pass or fail.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, these are the last questions now and they’re things that I asked you last time. It’s not a test, to see if you get the same answer, it’s just to see if your opinion has changed since your new experiences. So what five words would you used to describe the characteristics of the engineering industry and your experience of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The engineering industry, um… haphazard, in the way that it just – nothing ever goes to plan and you just have to muddle around and try and get the best out of it you can. Um, what else? Difficult, definitely, and complex, um… there’s not a word that can describe it, but I’d say sort of communication in terms of you need a lot of it, you know, to be able to communicate a lot and not in the way that I originally thought you’d have to, like for drawings and things, it’s more about talking and explaining and –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to do a lot of work explaining the engineering stuff to people that aren’t engineers or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it’s mainly – it’s mainly engineer to engineer here. I don’t think I've ever had to explain anything to a non-engineer. It’s getting used to the jargon that they use here, you know, like, ‘Ah, that’s a 50-mili bore such and such. Why are you using a road tool which is only 20-mili with a circumferential something or other or such and blah di blah’, you know. I mean it’s just ‘What?’ (inaudible) or a PCND or something, I don’t know, all this stuff they just come out with, they just (inaudible) I suppose if you’re in this industry it’s fine, but yeah. I think I’ve got one more word to think of, um… one more word about engineering… don’t know… varied, most definitely varied. It’s not all about technical, it’s not all about drawing, it’s not all about managerial, it’s not all about marketing, which I didn’t even think it was about marketing before, but it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Bit of everything.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, cost, materials, everything. And I think –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do any business type modules at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we did, um – yeah, we did, but it’s like we did, um, we did both business, quality and law, so it was like a double module with those three subjects in it – oh sorry, business law, quality and something or other, I forget. But there was this whole thing about manufacturing processes are supposed to conform to ISO standards and all this kind of stuff and they actually do that here, so it’s been interesting to see that being implemented. Um, and I did get a brief look into it in that I did have, um, that business process, um, management course I went on dealt with the same sort of things that I’ve been taught at uni, which was – but more concentrated on this business and it made a lot more sense. So, definitely varied. And I think as a person I’d rather be an all rounder instead of a design technician or a manufacturing person. I’d rather be able to sit there and be able to dabble.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’d rather be a generalist than a specialist.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Indeed, indeed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, we spoke a bit earlier about advantages, but do you think that there are any other advantages or any disadvantages now to being a woman in a male dominated…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, God like if you want to look nice and you wear like heels and the floor here, man they can here you coming a mile away, it’s just like (makes sound). So that’s quite bad. Um, in terms of, I don’t know, I don’t think so. Everyone – I think it’s the kind of workplace this is and the only reason why you’d stay here permanently for the rest of your life is probably one of those because of the people jobbies as opposed to you love the job so much, it’s going to be all the people here are really nice. Um, I don’t – I mean I might just be being completely blind here and not seeing that people are being sexist or something, but I’ve never experienced that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why then do you think that there maybe aren’t more women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I know it sounds a bit clichéd when they say that girls can’t think like guys, but it’s really true. It’s like there are certain things that I’ve found here that I’ve found a lot more difficult than other people and there are certain things I’m a lot better at. I’m a lot better at organising information, um, collecting information and all this kind of stuff, but as soon as you give me, um, give me something to, um, like find the solution to or like imagine you’re in a different sort of orientation or something, it takes a lot more brain power to do that. I can do it, it’s not that I can’t do it, I can do it, but it takes me a wee bit longer than perhaps someone else in the company and you know, that might just be because they’ve been here longer. There’s lots of things it might be, but I think something that I struggle with is thinking in a different way. Thinking out of the box, as they say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it matters then that there aren’t more women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, because I think the only reason why I find that difficult is because that’s the way this industry is set up to think as and I think that there may be another way of doing that may appeal to women. I think if you gave a woman the same job as a man she’d go about it in a completely different way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But she’d still get it done?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and it mightn’t be that one was better than the other, it would just be different, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got any ideas now about how more women could be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think it’s just getting it into schools and showing people, giving actual real examples and then having women go to schools and sort of say, ‘Well, you know what? I did this. It was a little bit hard, but look at the advantages I'm getting out of it.’ Showing the rewards that you can get from putting a bit more effort in, because I think for me to do – to do a job like a business job or a law job is a lot easier than doing an engineering job and all you need to do is make one more attractive than the other. Take the easy road or take the slightly harder road and get more benefits out of it. I think I can do the work, it might take me a little bit longer, it might be a little bit harder for me, but I can still do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that business and law are portrayed to the public as being more glamorous?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The law is. The law is because of all the TV shows. Um, business probably not so much. Business is the easy way out, but you see I find that if you do a subject like engineering you get a lot more respect from people. If you say, ‘I do law’ they go ‘Oh, you do law, great’. I mean and the big joke among the engineers at [university] is they’re doing Psychology. You know, you want to try a day doing our degree and see how you manage doing that, you know. We do this many hours and have this many exams and our course is so much harder than yours and – yeah, so I think it is, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that’s fantastic, thank you very much.
